## Status

Design only. Recorded by P-013 of `cupboard-distributable-integrations-2026-10-10` (decision D-008). Nothing here is built. Bring-your-own client registration (the generic registration form, P-009) and pasted credentials (`setup.credentials`, P-001) remain the supported paths.

## How OAuth providers resolve a client today

- A provider package declares `oauth` on its `ProviderDescriptor` (authorize and token URLs, scopes) and may name `clientRegistrationRef` (`packages/plugin-sdk/src/provider.ts`).
- The SDK refuses any key matching `/secret/i` inside `provider.oauth`, so a package can never carry a client secret.
- The host resolves the client in `resolveOAuthProvider` (`packages/operator-core/lib/integrations/connection-lifecycle.ts`): it reads the registration named by `clientRegistrationRef` (default: the provider group id) from the host-held `oauth-apps.json`, takes `clientSecret` or `clientSecretFile`, unions the scopes of every member of the group, and defaults the redirect to the operator's provider-neutral `/api/oauth/callback`.

So every user who installs an OAuth provider package must first create an OAuth app at the provider and register its client id and secret. That step is the friction a hosted client removes.

## Proposal

Papercusp operates one registered OAuth app per listed provider and exposes it to eligible packages as a host-provided registration, for example `clientRegistrationRef: "papercusp-hosted:<provider>"`. The card shows a single Connect button when the hosted registration applies, and the bring-your-own form otherwise.

### 1. Secret custody: a token broker

A confidential client secret cannot ship in the desktop binary or in a package. A Papercusp-hosted broker holds it and performs the code-for-token exchange and every refresh. The desktop starts the flow with PKCE and a `state` bound to the install; the broker exchanges the code, then returns tokens over TLS only to the install that holds the PKCE verifier. Providers that support public clients with PKCE and no secret need no broker for the exchange, only the redirect relay below.

### 2. Redirect relay

Provider apps require fixed redirect URIs. The hosted app registers the broker's HTTPS callback; the broker relays the result to the desktop through a loopback listener (`127.0.0.1` on an ephemeral port named in `state`) or the `papercusp://` deep link. The operator's `/api/oauth/callback` stays the redirect for bring-your-own registrations.

### 3. Eligibility and scope pinning

- Only packages listed in the Cupboard with a verified publisher signature may use a hosted registration.
- The hosted registration's scopes are pinned to the reviewed listing. A package version that requests scopes beyond its listing falls back to bring-your-own until the listing is re-reviewed.
- The host refuses a hosted registration for an unlisted, sideloaded or locally modified package.

### 4. Refresh and availability

Tokens are stored locally in the encrypted credential store. For confidential providers each refresh goes through the broker, which makes the broker an availability dependency: when it is unreachable, connections keep working until the access token expires, then show `reconnect_required` with a bring-your-own option.

### 5. Provider review and shared limits

One hosted app is shared by every Papercusp user of that provider, so it inherits each provider's distribution rules (for example Slack app distribution review, Google verification and security assessment for restricted scopes) and one shared rate-limit pool. The broker needs per-install quotas so one workspace cannot exhaust the pool.

### 6. Privacy

The broker sees authorization codes and tokens in transit. It must not log or persist them. A stronger variant encrypts tokens to the install's public key before returning them, so the broker never holds a usable token after the response.

### 7. Revocation and kill switch

The broker can disable a provider's hosted registration (credential leak, provider suspension, abuse). Users always keep the bring-your-own path, so disabling it degrades setup convenience, not capability.

## Open questions before building

- Who operates the broker (Papercusp cloud, or a self-hostable component for teams) and under which identity the provider apps are registered.
- Whether team installs share one hosted grant per workspace or authorize per user.
- How listing review records scope approval, so scope pinning has a machine-checkable source.

## When to revisit

Build this once the first-party `slack` and `bug-triage` packages ship through the Cupboard (P-011) and setup friction is measured on real installs, or when the owner asks for one-click setup.
